title: Neutropenia
subject: Medicine
summary: Neutropenia is a low absolute neutrophil count that raises infection risk. Diagnose with a CBC, stage severity, identify reversible causes, and manage promptly, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Neutropenia is defined by an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) < 1500/µL on a peripheral blood smear. Severe neutropenia is ANC < 500/µL; profound < 100/µL.
b: ANC = total WBC × (% neutrophils + % bands) / 100
Confirm with repeat CBC if patient is stable

t.b: What is the neutrophil count? – Confirms neutropenia and assesses other cytopenias

sections.p: Stage guides infection risk and urgency of intervention.
b: Mild: ANC 1000‑1499/µL
Moderate: ANC 500‑999/µL
Severe: ANC < 500/µL
Profound: ANC < 100/µL

sections.p: In East African low‑resource hospitals, think of infections, drugs, and marrow infiltration.
b: HIV infection (especially with opportunistic TB or cryptococcus)
Tuberculosis (bone marrow involvement or drug‑induced)
Malaria (splenic sequestration, drug toxicity)
Severe bacterial sepsis
Antiretroviral drugs (e.g., zidovudine)
Chemotherapy or anti‑TB drugs (e.g., rifampicin, isoniazid)
Herbal remedies containing bone‑marrow suppressants

sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic until infection occurs; look for fever, oral ulcers, skin pustules, or rapid deterioration.
b: Fever without source
Mucosal ulceration
Recurrent skin abscesses
Unexplained fatigue

sections.p: Targeted tests identify reversible causes and assess infection risk.

t.b: Is HIV present? – Positive test prompts ART review and prophylaxis
Is active TB present? – Positive result directs anti‑TB therapy, which may affect marrow
Are there immature cells or dysplasia? – Suggests marrow infiltration or drug effect
Is there a nutritional deficiency? – Low levels guide supplementation

sections.p: Severe neutropenia predisposes to life‑threatening infections.
b: Fever > 38°C lasting > 1 h
Rapidly expanding cellulitis or necrotizing fasciitis
Septic shock signs (hypotension, altered mental status)
Unexplained bleeding (possible marrow failure)

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, protect against infection, and consider growth‑factor support when resources allow.
b: Stop offending drugs (e.g., zidovudine) and switch to safer alternatives
Start empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics covering Pseudomonas for ANC < 500/µL with fever
Give G‑CSF (filgrastim) if available for profound neutropenia or anticipated chemotherapy‑induced drop
Implement strict hand hygiene, protective isolation if possible, and prophylactic cotrimoxazole for HIV‑positive patients

sections.p: Monitor ANC twice weekly until recovery; educate on infection avoidance.
b: Repeat CBC every 3‑5 days in severe cases
Vaccinate against pneumococcus and influenza when counts recover
Counsel on safe herbal use and nutrition

sections.p: Conditions that mimic low neutrophils on routine labs.
b: Leukopenia due to lymphopenia (different infection risk)
Laboratory artifact from clotted sample (pseudo‑neutropenia)

sections.p: Interpretation pitfalls in low‑resource labs.
b: Automated counters may misclassify immature cells as lymphocytes, under‑estimating neutropenia
Severe anemia can falsely lower calculated ANC; verify with manual differential

faq.q: Why is neutropenia more dangerous in HIV patients?
faq.a: HIV impairs cell‑mediated immunity; low neutrophils further reduce bacterial defence, raising sepsis risk.
Yes, severe malaria can suppress marrow and cause drug‑induced neutropenia from antimalarials.
For profound neutropenia (<100/µL) with fever, or when chemotherapy is expected to cause a severe drop and supportive care is possible.

exam: A 35‑year‑old HIV‑positive man presents with fever and ANC 400/µL – what is your immediate management? — Start empiric anti‑pseudomonal β‑lactam, assess for source, consider G‑CSF if available.
How does severe neutropenia change your interpretation of a normal chest X‑ray? — Recognise that infection may be present despite a clear film; rely on clinical signs and early cultures.
Which drug commonly used in East Africa can cause neutropenia and should be stopped? — Zidovudine; replace with a less myelotoxic regimen.
What laboratory finding would suggest bone‑marrow infiltration rather than drug effect? — Presence of immature granulocytes >20% of total neutrophils or pancytopenia on CBC.
Why is prophylactic cotrimoxazole recommended in neutropenic HIV patients? — It prevents Pneumocystis jirovecii and bacterial infections, reducing mortality.
A patient on anti‑TB therapy develops neutropenia; what is the next step? — Review for isoniazid or rifampicin toxicity, consider temporary drug hold, and monitor ANC closely.
Explain why a low ANC does not always require G‑CSF in low‑resource settings. — Cost, limited availability, and modest benefit unless ANC <100/µL with infection.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt urgent referral to a tertiary centre? — Fever with hypotension or rapidly progressing cellulitis despite antibiotics.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and systematic physical exam identify reversible causes, infection risk and clues to marrow infiltration in low‑resource settings.
b: Recent or current infections (TB, malaria, bacterial sepsis); fever pattern and source; HIV status and CD4 count; recent chemotherapy, anti‑TB drugs, antiretrovirals, antibiotics, herbal remedies; drug start dates and any dose changes; nutritional status and recent weight loss; exposure to radiation or chemicals; family history of hematologic disease; pregnancy status; recent v

t.b: Look for pallor, jaundice, bruising, petechiae, oral ulcers, skin pustules or necrotic lesions; presence suggests infection, marrow failure or peripheral destruction.
Document fever (>38 °C) or hypothermia; fever in neutropenia mandates urgent antibiotics.
Inspect oral cavity for ulcers, thrush, gingival bleeding; positive findings raise suspicion for opportunistic infection or severe neutropenia.
Enlarged nodes may indicate infection, lymphoma or TB; a negative exam does not exclude marrow disease.
Tenderness, hepatosplenomegaly suggest infiltration or sepsis; splenomegaly points toward hypersplenism or infection.
Assess perfusion; delayed refill may reflect sepsis despite low ANC.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Select tests that answer a specific clinical question; when a test is unavailable, use the next best alternative or clinical judgment.
b: Complete blood count with differential – confirms ANC, assesses anemia and thrombocytopenia; repeat after 12‑24 h if stable.

t.b: ANC = total WBC × (% neutrophils + % bands)/100; guides severity staging and infection risk.
Look for dysplastic granules, blasts, parasites; presence of blasts suggests leukemia, parasites suggest malaria.

t.a: HIV rapid test or viral load
t.b: Positive test confirms HIV‑related neutropenia; low CD4 (<200) increases infection risk.
Rule out pneumonia; a normal film does not exclude early infection in neutropenia.
Detect bacteremia; positive culture directs targeted antibiotics.
Identify organ dysfunction that may modify drug choice; elevated bilirubin limits certain antibiotics.
Elevated levels support bacterial infection; low levels do not rule out fungal infection in ANC < 500.
Detect urinary source; leukocyte‑negative urine in neutropenia may still harbor infection.
Rapid detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis; positive result guides anti‑TB regimen.
If ANC < 500 and fever persists >4 days, positive test suggests invasive fungal infection; unavailable tests → empirical antifungal therapy.

sections.p: Classification is based on ANC and clinical context; it directs urgency of antimicrobial therapy and need for growth‑factor support.
b: Mild neutropenia: ANC 1000‑1499 µL – monitor, treat underlying cause, no routine prophylaxis.
Moderate neutropenia: ANC 500‑999 µL – increased infection vigilance, consider prophylaxis only if additional risk factors (e.g., HIV CD4 < 200).
Severe neutropenia: ANC <500 µL – high infection risk, start empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics promptly; evaluate for G‑CSF if febrile or deteriorating.

sections.p: Several disorders mimic neutropenia or share overlapping signs; careful history, targeted tests and bedside clues separate them.

t.b: Pancytopenia, hypocellular marrow, no blasts; history of drug exposure, viral hepatitis; bone‑marrow biopsy shows empty marrow.
Splenomegaly with cytopenias; peripheral smear may show target cells; ultrasound confirms enlarged spleen; ANC low due to sequestration.

t.a: Severe bacterial sepsis with neutrophil margination
t.b: Transient ANC drop, often normal marrow; rapid rise after infection control; blood cultures positive.
Sudden ANC <500 after drug start; no marrow dysplasia; improvement after drug withdrawal.
Blasts >20 % on smear, anemia, thrombocytopenia; bone‑marrow aspirate hypercellular with blasts; requires oncology referral.
History of recent malaria, splenomegaly, parasites on smear; ANC may be low but recovers after antimalarial therapy.

sections.p: A systematic ladder guides safe care from immediate stabilisation to definitive therapy, monitoring, and timely escalation or referral.
b: 1. Assess airway, breathing, circulation; give supplemental O₂ if SpO₂ < 94 %.
2. Obtain two sets of blood cultures before any antibiotics; draw CBC with differential and basic metabolic panel.
3. Start empiric broad‑spectrum IV anti‑pseudomonal β‑lactam (e.g., cefepime or meropenem) immediately in any febrile patient (ANC < 500 µL).
4. Add oral/IV fluoroquinolone or aminoglycoside only if local resistance patterns dictate or if patient is unstable.
5. Discontinue any suspected offending drug (e.g., zidovudine, anti‑TB agents) as soon as neutropenia is recognised and alternative therapy is available.
6. Consider G‑CSF (filgrastim) for ANC < 500 µL with persistent fever, clinical deterioration, or when rapid marrow recovery is essential (e.g., pending chemotherapy).

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Recognising adverse drug reactions and interactions prevents worsening neutropenia and guides corrective actions.
b: Zidovudine: bone‑marrow suppression; stop drug, switch to alternative NRTI, monitor ANC weekly.
Chemotherapy agents (e.g., cyclophosphamide): dose‑dependent marrow toxicity; use G‑CSF prophylactically when cumulative dose high.
Trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole: can cause agranulocytosis; discontinue, treat with supportive antibiotics, avoid re‑exposure.
Herbal remedies containing aristolochic acid or heavy metals: may suppress marrow; obtain detailed medication history, advise cessation, consider toxicology screen.
Concurrent nephrotoxic drugs (e.g., aminoglycosides) with G‑CSF: increase risk of renal injury; monitor creatinine, adjust dosing.

sections.p: Neutropenia predisposes to rapid infection spread; early recognition of complications triggers higher‑level care.
b: Ecthyma gangrenosum or necrotizing skin lesions → urgent surgical consult, broaden antibiotics to include anti‑pseudomonal coverage.
Severe mucositis with oral ulcers causing inability to ingest → consider IV hydration, analgesia, and antifungal prophylaxis.
Signs of sepsis (hypotension, lactate > 2 mmol/L, altered mental status) → activate sepsis bundle, transfer to ICU.
Development of organ dysfunction (renal failure, respiratory distress) while neutropenic → immediate escalation to higher‑level facility.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities and local exposures modify presentation, laboratory interpretation, and therapeutic choices.
b: HIV: CD4 < 200 cells/µL amplifies infection risk; cotrimoxazole prophylaxis mandatory, consider opportunistic pathogens (Cryptococcus, CMV).
Active TB: marrow infiltration or drug toxicity; obtain sputum GeneXpert, consider bone‑marrow biopsy if cytopenias persist.
Malnutrition: low albumin may mask infection severity; give high‑protein nutrition, monitor electrolytes.
Pregnancy: avoid teratogenic drugs (e.g., certain fluoroquinolones); use β‑lactam plus macrolide if needed, adjust G‑CSF dosing cautiously.
Diabetes mellitus: hyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil function; optimise glucose, watch for fungal infections.
Renal or hepatic failure: dose‑adjust antibiotics, avoid nephrotoxic agents, monitor drug levels where possible.
Age extremes: infants have higher baseline ANC; elderly may have blunted febrile response; use lower thresholds for escalation.

sections.p: Tailored approaches address physiological differences and resource constraints.
b: Children: use age‑adjusted ANC cut‑offs (e.g., <1500 µL still neutropenic); prioritize oral antibiotics for low‑risk fever, avoid radiation exposure in imaging.
Pregnant women: choose category B antibiotics, defer G‑CSF unless life‑threatening infection, monitor fetal growth.
Elderly: higher prevalence of polypharmacy; review all meds for marrow toxicity, start empiric therapy early due to atypical presentation.
People with HIV in low‑resource settings: prioritize cotrimoxazole prophylaxis, use generic ceftriaxone if β‑lactam unavailable, rely on clinical sepsis scores.

Low‑resource hospitals: if CBC unavailable, use total white‑cell count and differential smear; if cultures not possible, treat empirically based on local antibiogram and add antifungal if fever >7 days.

sections.p: Practice items covering history, examination, investigations, management, complications and special‑population considerations.
b: 1. Which bedside question best identifies drug‑induced neutropenia? (Answer: recent start or dose change of known marrow‑suppressive agents).
2. How do you perform a focused skin exam for ecthyma gangrenosum? (Inspect for painless black eschar with surrounding erythema; palpate for induration; positive sign suggests Pseudomonas sepsis).
4. When should G‑CSF be initiated in a febrile neutropenic patient? (ANC < 500 µL with persistent fever >48 h or clinical deterioration).
5. How does severe malnutrition alter ANC interpretation? (Low baseline ANC may be physiologic; use clinical infection signs rather than strict cut‑offs).
6. Which antibiotic regimen is recommended for empiric therapy in a HIV‑positive patient with ANC = 400 µL and fever? (IV anti‑pseudomonal β‑lactam plus oral cotrimoxazole prophylaxis).
7. What is the next step if a patient on rifampicin develops ANC = 80 µL? (Stop rifampicin, substitute with alternative TB drug, consider G‑CSF if febrile).
8. Define febrile neutropenia and its significance in oncology patients. (Temperature ≥ 38.3 °C or ≥ 38.0 °C sustained for 1 h with ANC < 500 µL; indicates high risk of rapid sepsis).
9. How would you manage a low‑risk febrile neutropenic adult in a district hospital without inpatient beds? (Oral fluoroquinolone, close outpatient follow‑up, educate on return precautions).
10. In a pre‑term neonate with NEC suspicion, does neutropenia affect Bell’s staging? (No; Bell’s staging relies on clinical, radiologic, and laboratory signs of intestinal injury, not ANC).

facts: Febrile neutropenia: single oral temperature ≥38.3°C or ≥38.0°C sustained for ≥1 h
Common drug causes in East Africa: zidovudine, rifampicin, isoniazid, anti‑malarial agents, herbal bone‑marrow suppressants
HIV‑related neutropenia risk rises when CD4 <200 cells/µL
G‑CSF indicated for ANC <500/µL with fever or clinical deterioration
Prophylactic cotrimoxazole reduces bacterial and Pneumocystis infection in HIV neutropenia

mnemonics.t: Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol – first‑line TB drugs, each can cause marrow suppression
Zidovudine, Isoniazid, Dapsone – antiretroviral and anti‑TB agents frequently implicated in neutropenia

vivas.q: Define neutropenia and give the formula to calculate ANC.
vivas.a: Neutropenia is ANC <1500/µL; ANC = total WBC × (% neutrophils + % bands) / 100.

vivas.q: What is the immediate management of a febrile HIV‑positive patient with ANC 400/µL?
vivas.a: Start empiric IV anti‑pseudomonal antibiotics (e.g., cefepime), obtain blood cultures, give G‑CSF, and admit for monitoring.

vivas.q: Why does a normal chest X‑ray carry less reassurance in severe neutropenia?
vivas.a: Neutropenic patients may have early invasive bacterial infection without radiographic changes; a normal film does not exclude pneumonia.

vivas.q: Which anti‑TB drug most commonly causes neutropenia and should be stopped first?
vivas.a: Rifampicin – it suppresses marrow; discontinue and substitute with alternative regimen.

vivas.q: What laboratory finding suggests bone‑marrow infiltration rather than drug effect?
vivas.a: A leuko‑erythroblastic picture with circulating nucleated red cells and immature myeloid forms.

vivas.q: Why is prophylactic cotrimoxazole recommended in neutropenic HIV patients?
vivas.a: It prevents bacterial sepsis and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, both common when neutrophils are low.

vivas.q: A patient on anti‑TB therapy develops neutropenia; what is the next step?
vivas.a: Stop the suspected drug (usually rifampicin), start G‑CSF if ANC <500/µL with fever, and switch to a non‑myelotoxic regimen.

vivas.q: Explain why G‑CSF is not always given in low‑resource settings for neutropenia.
vivas.a: Cost and limited supply restrict use; focus on infection control, antibiotics, and removing offending drugs first.

vivas.q: What red‑flag symptom mandates urgent referral to a tertiary centre?
vivas.a: Persistent high‑grade fever (>38.5°C) despite 48 h of appropriate antibiotics or signs of sepsis (hypotension, tachypnea).

vivas.q: A patient with neutropenia develops ecthyma gangrenosum; which organism and toxin are responsible?
vivas.a: Pseudomonas aeruginosa producing exotoxin A, which inhibits protein synthesis.

vivas.q: Which Candida albicans transition enhances endothelial invasion?
vivas.a: Yeast‑to‑hyphal transition, allowing tissue penetration and biofilm formation.

vivas.q: How is a preterm neonate with neutropenia and left shift classified under Bell’s staging?
vivas.a: Bell’s staging does not use neutropenia; classification is based on clinical, radiologic, and laboratory signs of intestinal injury.

vivas.q: What syndrome links rheumatoid arthritis, neutropenia, and splenomegaly?
vivas.a: Felty’s syndrome – RA with neutropenia and splenomegaly.

vivas.q: Which intervention specifically stimulates bone‑marrow neutrophil production?
vivas.a: Granulocyte‑colony stimulating factor (G‑CSF).

vivas.q: How can overwhelming bacterial infection cause peripheral neutropenia?
vivas.a: Neutrophils marginate and migrate into infected tissues, and cytokine‑mediated sequestration reduces circulating count.

vivas.q: What marrow finding distinguishes ineffective granulopoiesis from drug‑induced suppression?
vivas.a: Hypercellular marrow with maturation arrest (ineffective) versus hypocellular marrow with reduced precursors (drug‑induced).

vivas.q: Classify an ANC of 0.7 × 10⁹/L.
vivas.a: Moderate neutropenia (ANC 500‑999/µL).

vivas.q: List the ANC severity categories and their typical management implications.
vivas.a: Mild (1000‑1499): monitor; Moderate (500‑999): monitor, consider infection work‑up; Severe (<500): start antibiotics, consider G‑CSF; Profound (<100): urgent broad‑spectrum antibiotics, G‑CSF, possible isolation.

vivas.q: Define febrile neutropenia and its significance in cancer patients.
vivas.a: Fever ≥38.3°C or ≥38.0°C sustained ≥1 h with ANC <500/µL; indicates high risk of rapid sepsis and mandates immediate broad‑spectrum antibiotics.

vivas.q: When a neutropenic patient remains febrile after ANC recovery, what should be considered?
vivas.a: Persistent infection, drug‑resistant organisms, fungal infection, or non‑infectious causes such as drug fever; broaden antimicrobial coverage and obtain further cultures.

mcqs.q: A 28‑year‑old HIV patient on zidovudine presents with ANC 450/µL and fever 38.5°C. Which is the best next step?
o: Continue zidovudine and start oral amoxicillin
Observe and repeat CBC in 48 h
Stop zidovudine, start IV anti‑pseudomonal antibiotics and give G‑CSF
mcqs.e: Severe neutropenia with fever requires drug withdrawal, IV broad‑spectrum antibiotics, and G‑CSF.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical cause of neutropenia in East African low‑resource hospitals?
mcqs.e: Ivermectin is not commonly associated with neutropenia.

mcqs.q: A patient on chemotherapy has ANC 80/µL but is afebrile. What is the first action?
o: Hold chemotherapy and monitor; no G‑CSF needed if stable
mcqs.e: In afebrile stable patients, stop the myelotoxic agent and monitor; G‑CSF is reserved for fever or clinical decline.

mcqs.q: Which sign is most reliable for detecting ascites at the bedside?
mcqs.e: Shifting dullness demonstrates fluid movement with patient position change.

mcqs.q: In a neutropenic patient, a leuko‑erythroblastic smear suggests:
mcqs.e: Presence of nucleated RBCs and immature myeloid cells points to infiltration.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is the recommended prophylaxis for Pneumocystis jirovecii in HIV patients with neutropenia?
mcqs.e: Cotrimoxazole provides coverage for PCP and many bacterial pathogens.

mcqs.q: A neonate with left shift and neutropenia is being staged for NEC. Which factor is NOT part of Bell’s staging?
mcqs.e: Bell’s staging does not incorporate neutrophil count.

mcqs.q: Which drug class directly stimulates neutrophil production?
mcqs.e: G‑CSF is the specific agent that drives neutrophil maturation.

cases.v: A 42‑year‑old man with known HIV (CD4 150) presents with fever 38.7°C, oral ulcers, and ANC 380/µL. Blood cultures pending.

qs.q: Which bedside examination finding would raise suspicion for a fungal infection?
qs.a: Persistent oral thrush with white plaques that cannot be scraped off, or new skin nodules with necrotic centers.

qs.q: If cultures later grow Pseudomonas aeruginosa, what additional therapy is indicated?
qs.a: Add an anti‑pseudomonal beta‑lactam (e.g., cefepime) if not already given; consider combination with an aminoglycoside for severe sepsis.

cases.v: A 30‑week gestation pregnant woman on rifampicin‑based TB therapy develops ANC 420/µL and mild cough, no fever.

qs.q: What is the first step in management?
qs.a: Stop rifampicin, substitute with an alternative TB drug (e.g., streptomycin or fluoroquinolone if safe), and monitor ANC.

qs.q: Which investigation helps differentiate drug effect from marrow infiltration?
qs.a: Bone‑marrow aspirate showing cellularity; a hypocellular marrow suggests drug effect, while infiltrative cells suggest disease.

mistakes: Assuming a normal chest X‑ray rules out pneumonia in severe neutropenia.
Starting G‑CSF for any neutropenia without considering fever or clinical deterioration.
Classifying ANC 0.7 × 10⁹/L as severe rather than moderate.
Continuing a suspected myelotoxic drug while adding G‑CSF in an afebrile patient.
Using neutropenia as a criterion for Bell’s NEC staging.
Prescribing prophylactic antibiotics for all moderate neutropenia without risk assessment.
Failing to stop the offending drug before initiating other interventions.
Confusing the ANC threshold for fungal infection concern (it is <500/µL, not >500/µL).
